It is exactly 0 on 63,274 of the 1,523,504 test rows, 2 of them laundering, where the probability is below float32's resolution; the log-loss clips at 1e-15, so each of those 2 costs 34.5 nats. The training run's booster, which keeps them above zero, scored the raw log-loss 0.00475425 where the graph scores 0.00475425, and the calibrated 0.00449744 where the graph scores 0.00449744; the Brier scores agree to 8 decimals.
calibration.reliability_diagram_defensible_here: YES on the test split, which carries 2,321 events and 1,521,183 non-events. Van Calster et al. (J Clin Epidemiol 2016) ask for at least 200 of each before a flexible calibration curve, and Riley et al. (Stat Med 2021) show that such rules of thumb can still be too few. NO on the browser's evaluation sample, drawn from the same window with fewer than 200 events, which is why the page draws no curve there and says so. The CORP terms are reported regardless, because pool-adjacent-violators picks no bin count, so they are stable where a binned curve is not.

calibration.why_not_isotonic: Measured in the run that wrote this record, on the teacher's own windows. The map raises the Brier score from 0.00077072 to 0.00082539 and lowers the log-loss from 0.00475425 to 0.00449744 on the test window, where 0.152% of rows are laundering; on the validation rows it was fitted on, 0.113% of them laundering, it lowers the Brier score from 0.00070321 to 0.00061622. Isotonic regression fitted on the same validation rows scores Brier 0.00081774, below Platt's, and log-loss 0.00450874, above Platt's; lower is better on both. Platt is kept as a choice, not as the better score: it is strictly monotone and two floats the browser applies, while isotonic ties the test window's 32,828 distinct scores at 97 values, 63,274 rows at exactly zero, 2 of them laundering, and it is the method of the student's and the networks' records, so the finance records differ by the model and not by the map.

not_measured.published_source: PGS Catalog PPM002038 for PGS000072: AUROC 0.637 (no confidence interval recorded), incident breast cancer in n=216,273 European-ancestry women in UK Biobank - 4,760 cases and 211,513 controls - from Kachuri et al., Nat Commun 11:6084 (2020), doi:10.1038/s41467-020-19600-4. A CITATION AND NOT A TARGET, for three reasons the record itself gives: the model is fitted WITH COVARIATES (age at assessment, family history of breast cancer, genotyping array, PCs 1-15, parity, age at menarche, body mass index, menopausal status, hormone replacement therapy, oral contraceptive use, alcohol intake, and body mass index by menopausal status), which a bare weighted dot product does not have; it used 'only 162 of the original 187 SNPs'; and it is an AUC at 5 years. It is the only AUROC among the score's three Catalog performance records; the other two report an odds ratio per standard deviation of 1.26 (95% CI 1.24-1.28; PPM000192, GERA and UK Biobank, n=237,549, Graff et al. 2021) and a hazard ratio of 1.26 (1.20-1.32; PPM017165, post-menopausal breast cancer, UK Biobank, n=1,990; Byrne et al., Int J Epidemiol 52:817-826, 2023).
not_measured.reason: 1000 Genomes is a reference panel with no breast-cancer case/control status. AUROC requires a phenotyped cohort, so the published figure is carried as a citation, not as a measurement from this run: 0.637 (AUROC (European ancestry)).

medical_fl.student.baseline_gap_note: This scores far below the 0.901 ResNet-18 baseline. The reason is representational rather than cryptographic: 3,226 parameters over a 14x14 input is a REPRESENTATION choice, not a feasibility limit - and this note said 'a CKKS-feasibility budget' until Round 32, which overstated how forced it was. Kim et al. (arXiv:2506.15258) do HE chest-X-ray inference on a VQGAN latent at downsampling factor 8 rather than on pixels, so the alternative to downsampling 28->14 is re-representing the input. The browser already runs onnxruntime-web, so such an encoder would run locally in plaintext with no privacy loss. Recorded as the sixth falsifiable trigger in the additional-model decision in docs/deliverable-verification.md, not acted on - and note that f=8 on a 28x28 input gives 3.5x3.5, so the transfer is the open measurement rather than a citation. This sentence claimed the trigger existed for two rounds while the table held five rows and none of them was this one; the trigger was written, and the decision moved to a tracked file so the claim can be checked. Round 24 found it had been WORSE than that - a constant predictor, emitting one class for all 156 test images, with accuracy 0.730769 exactly equal to the majority-class rate and AUC 0.354, below random. It was invisible because the registry declared `auc` while the record stored `accuracy`, and because this student had neither protection its teacher already had: class-weighted loss and AUC-based model selection. Both were added. Read `n_classes_predicted` and `majority_class_rate` beside the score - an accuracy equal to the majority rate is the signature of a model that learned nothing. Workings: references/medical-student-collapse-investigation.md.
medical_fl.student.metric_note: Two metrics are recorded and they answer different questions. `auc` is the registry's declared headline and is what the published baseline compares against. `student_metric`/`teacher_metric` are accuracy, because fidelity compares DECISIONS and a decision has no score to rank - so agreement and metric_delta are necessarily computed on a decision metric. Do not read the accuracy against the AUC baseline.

satellite_comms.telemanom.baseline_gap_note: Read n_events_scored before comparing this to the baseline. Since Round 86 the forecaster follows ESA-ADB's Telemanom-ESA recipe on its own Mission1 split: a 30 s zero-order hold, training only on unlabelled windows before 2007-01-01 with early stopping on the months from 2006-10-01, a 10-step forecast scored on its first step, and Telemanom's thresholding per channel. The half after the split holds 29 labelled anomalies of the 51 on these channels. This score is the plain zero-order hold at an error floor of 0.0105 raw units, chosen on the validation months, which hold 2 anomalies: tp=23 fp=0 fn=6, 8,069 of 7,364,160 points flagged. The published 0.968 is Telemanom-ESA-Pruned, whose floor of 0.05/7 the paper does not show was chosen without the test half, and it is scored on ESA-ADB's prepared series, which writes annotated samples the zero-order hold dropped back onto the grid - a step that reads the labels. Replicating both gives 0.968 (tp=25 fp=0 fn=4), and 0.791 over all events but communication gaps, where Table 2 prints 0.786 (28 of 65 events here; the published recall 0.424 is no whole number of events out of this count, so ESA-ADB's all-events set differs from this selection by at least one event); esa_scores holds every arm and floor. Remaining differences: PyTorch where ESA-ADB uses Keras, from Keras's initialisers, one seed, and ESA-ADB's per-file resampling at the split. Until Round 86 this model trained at 300 s on a 70/30 cut holding 3 events and flagged 2 of 441,600 points. Workings: references/satellite-event-count-investigation.md.

satellite_comms.telemanom.metric_note: ESA-ADB's event-wise F0.5 for anomalies alone, scored by a reimplementation of its ESAScores: an anomaly is detected when any flagged event intersects it, and a flagged event is a false positive only when it intersects no annotated event of any category. corrected_event_wise_f0_5 multiplies event precision by the time-level true-negative rate, as ESA-ADB reports it; event_wise_f0_5 does not. Telemanom's paper prints 0.71 under F0.5 in its Table 2, though its own precision and recall there (87.5% and 80.0% overall) give 0.86. point_adjusted_f1 is shown only to expose how much point adjustment inflates: Kim et al. (AAAI 2022) show that under point adjustment even a random anomaly score can reach state-of-the-art. Only labels whose ESA-ADB Category is 'Anomaly' count as positives; the 63 rare nominal events annotated on these six channels do not.
satellite_comms.telemanom.sample_size_note: Read n_events_scored before comparing this to a published figure. The denominator of an event-wise metric is EVENTS: 29 anomalies in this test half, so one event either way moves the score by a visible step. n_anomaly_intervals counts label ROWS, one per channel an anomaly touches (320); n_anomaly_events_timeline counts the anomalies themselves (51). The number is reported as measured rather than reweighted, with the sample size beside it so the comparison is not made silently.

telecom_ids.nidd.baseline_gap_note: There is no baseline number to have a gap to, and that is a deliberate registry decision rather than a missing measurement: the two figures usually quoted for this corpus (99.61% for a classical CNN, 99.71% for a hybrid quantum-classical Quan-ConvCNN, Wang/Fok/Thing) are ACCURACIES on the BINARY benign-versus-malicious task, and this model is judged on 9-class macro F1, so putting them in `baseline` would render an accuracy beside a macro F1 as though the two were the same scale. WHAT THE COMPARISON CAN AND CANNOT SAY. The 9-class anchors are the dataset paper's random forest at 99.48% accuracy on its top-10 features (Samarakoon et al., arXiv:2212.01298) and BiTAD (Future Internet 17(11) 482) at 0.9047. This model's 0.9979 is on 934,361 rows and its own stratified random split, and those figures are on the rows as published, so each is an anchor and not a head-to-head. WHAT THE ROWS SAY ABOUT THOSE FIGURES. On the 1,215,890 rows as published, inputs equal on the two copies of the flood cannot pass 0.7685, binary or nine-class, so a score above that rests on a column that differs between the copies. Those are `Unnamed: 0`, `Rank`, `Seq`, `Offset` and `IdleTime`. The dataset paper's top-10 inputs include `Seq` and `Offset`. Of Wang/Fok/Thing's 28 inputs exactly one, `Offset`, differs between the copies, and `published_inputs_check` fits this project's booster to them: on the binary task accuracy 0.9599 with `Offset` and 0.7643 without it. That measures what those columns can do on these rows and does not rerun those papers' models. Wang/Fok/Thing's fall across base stations, from above 98% to 78.23% and 74.28% for the classical CNN, has the same shape here: with the copies in place this booster scores 0.4199 and 0.6059, and with them out 0.9973 and 0.9877.

contradictory_copies.what_this_means: The published file holds the same 281,529 flows twice. The first base station's UDP-flood file also holds the traffic of the second base station's attacker towards the victim, labelled Benign; the second base station's file holds those flows labelled UDPFlood. The two copies agree on every column but the labels and the file-position columns, and in the two capture files the 421,471 packets behind them carry identical timestamps, which two separate capture points could not produce. In each attack file exactly one address pair carries the attack label, which is why the second attacker's flows came out Benign in the first file. On these rows no model reading flow statistics can pass 1 - 281,529 / 1,215,890 = 0.7685. The loader keeps the UDPFlood copy, which is what the traffic was, and removes the Benign one; `as_published` repeats the same fit without that removal.

export.int8_skipped_reason: tree ensemble: parameters live in node attributes, not weight tensors, so dynamic int8 quantisation has nothing to quantise

file_label_counterfactual.what_this_means: `IdleTime` holds 17 values, all multiples of 128, the spacing of a 32-bit float at this size, one for each attack session and base station. Read as Unix times they fall between 13 and 15 September 2022, and the dataset paper gives the captures as 26 and 29 August 2022, so the column does not measure anything about the flow: it names the file the flow came from, and each file is one attack. On the rows as published it was worth about 22 accuracy points, because it is one of the few columns that differs between the two copies of the flood described under `contradictory_copies`. On the cleaned rows it adds what is measured here, and that gain is still a model recognising the file. The shipped model does not read it.

telecom_ids.nidd.framing: Real 5G network traffic, 9 attack classes, 46 flow-statistic features. This is a NETWORK-LAYER model and a different task from the QKD-layer classifier on the same page - no shared labels, no shared features, so the two scores are not a comparison. TWO CORRECTIONS MADE IN ROUND 86 EXPLAIN THE NUMBERS. The published file holds one attacker's UDP flood twice, the same 281,529 flows labelled Benign in one base station's file and UDPFlood in the other's; the Benign copies are removed, leaving 934,361 flows. And the model no longer reads `IdleTime`, which names the attack-session file a flow came from. Accuracy is 0.9979 and macro F1 0.9972. On the rows as published the same fit scores accuracy 0.7616, and no model reading these columns could pass 0.7685 there (`contradictory_copies`). `file_label_counterfactual` and `leak_counterfactual_accuracy` restore bookkeeping columns and reach about 1.0000, which is not a better model but a leak. `cross_base_station` trains on one base station and tests on the other: accuracy 0.9973 and 0.9877, against 0.4199 and 0.6059 on the rows as published. Two weak spots remain. Trained on the second base station, SYNFlood on the first scores F1 0.22. And without the TTL and hop columns, UDPScan across base stations falls to F1 0.05 (`without_ttl_and_hops`).

linear_baseline.what_it_is: multinomial logistic regression on the 36 NUMERIC features only, standardised, fitted directly rather than distilled. The 10 ordinal codes are excluded because their integer order is nominal and a linear model would read it as a magnitude. Recorded as the classical floor and as a feasibility probe for a future CKKS-linear tier: it predicts 9 of 9 classes, so a linear student on this corpus does not collapse the way an 8-class one nearly does elsewhere in this project.

telecom_ids.nidd.metric_note: macro F1 and aggregate accuracy agree here, 0.9972 and 0.9979, and neither is the flattering one. They were far apart until the contradictory copies came out, 0.9275 against 0.7616, because the contradiction fell on the two largest classes. macro F1 stays the headline because the largest class is about 400 times the smallest. Read `per_class_f1` for what the two averages hide: SlowrateDoS is lowest at 0.9873, HTTPFlood is at 0.9934, and ICMPFlood, at 289 test rows, is at 0.9983. A linear model on the numeric columns reaches accuracy 0.9838 and macro F1 0.9691, so most of this is separable by a plane, which is what a corpus where each class came from its own tool against its own service should look like. The random split is the easier test: see `cross_base_station`.

published_inputs_check.model: this project's booster, 300 trees, a 70/30 split at seed 42

telecom_ids.nidd.sample_size_note: Trained and scored on 5G-NIDD BTS1_BTS2_fields_preserved.csv with the 281,529 Benign-labelled copies of one attacker's flood removed: 934,361 of its 1,215,890 flows, stratified 75/25 at seed 42, so the test split is 233,591 rows and every class keeps its proportion among the remaining rows. Row for row the file is the same corpus as Combined.csv, which this model used until Round 50; only the column count differs, 113 against 52. No subsampling and no class rebalancing: `ICMPFlood` is 1,155 rows in the corpus and 289 in the test split, which is small but is the real prevalence, and resampling it would report a per-class F1 for a distribution the deployed model never sees. The browser evaluation sample is a different matter and is NOT proportional - see the note in eval_sample.json, which states its per-class floor and why its macro F1 is not this one.

single_feature_leak_check.what_this_means: One-vs-rest rank-AUC per feature per class, at the 0.90 threshold scripts/prep_model_inputs.py already publishes against, measured AFTER all 67 drops. A LARGE NUMBER HERE IS EXPECTED ON THIS CORPUS AND IS NOT THE LEAK THIS MODEL IS ABOUT. The attacks are generated by distinct tools against distinct services, so a scan, a SYN flood and a slow-rate HTTP attack genuinely differ in TTL, packet rate, TCP window and ACK timing - these are the flow statistics an intrusion detector is supposed to use. The check's own docstring anticipates the case and warns rather than failing. The distinction that matters is against `leak_counterfactual_*`: `Unnamed: 0`, `Rank`, `Seq` and `Offset` cleared the same threshold while being bookkeeping columns that carry no information about the traffic at all, which is why those four are dropped and these are kept. The check cannot tell a file label from a statistic: `IdleTime` is out because its values name the attack session's file, which only reading the values showed, and `file_label_counterfactual` records what it was worth. Recorded rather than described so the distinction is checkable.

telecom_ids.qml.classical_rf_attribution_note: Impurity importance (training split, biased toward high-cardinality features) and permutation importance (held-out split, scored on macro F1, 20 repeats, std reported). Read the permutation figure where they disagree. These rank which features of a SYNTHETIC corpus this forest needs, not signals from a real QKD link. Two planted features are nearly redundant: sift_ratio separates detector_blinding perfectly on its own yet costs almost nothing to remove, because click_asymmetry separates the same class; and dark_count_rate is within one std of zero. Exact linear SHAP does not apply to a tree ensemble, which is why these two measures are used instead.

telecom_ids.qml.dataset: QKD attack telemetry (synthetic, signatures of this project's own design)

telecom_ids.qml.framing: Architecture comparison, not a performance claim. The published model is the random forest; the quantum-kernel SVC and the variational QNN are recorded beside it and not published. The data is synthetic because no commercial-OK real QKD-attack corpus exists. Published QML-IDS results are mixed rather than uniformly below a random forest: Al-Kuwari et al. (arXiv:2509.14282) report a hybrid QLSTM at 94.7% against their own random forest, while arXiv:2512.05069 was withdrawn by its own authors for insufficient evaluation. Per-class F1 is the headline; aggregate accuracy is shown beside it because Engelen et al. (WTMC 2021) demonstrated it stays at 0.99 across a label correction that moved Bot F1 from 0.60 to 0.99.

quantum_comparison_like_for_like.basis: binary attack-against-normal macro F1, each quantum model against a forest trained and scored on that model's own split and labels

telecom_ids.student.argmax_location: client, in plaintext, after decrypting all 8 class scores
telecom_ids.student.metric_note: Read `n_classes_predicted` before `macro_f1`. A linear student that stops predicting a class scores 0 on it by construction, and macro F1 then averages in a zero that looks like poor discrimination rather than an absent output - this repo's own QNN carries exactly that defect and is documented as doing so, so the check is not hypothetical. `agreement` is recorded but is NOT evidence the minority classes survived: agreement on the finance student rose from 0.884 to 0.947 across a change that left minority-class F1 unmoved, which is why per-class F1 is the headline here and the aggregate is a companion.
